title: Trust as a Trajectory Property: An Epistemic Dynamics Framework for AI Evaluation
content: Trustworthy deployment of AI systems under uncertainty requires more than accurate predictions: it requires structured mechanisms for confidence estimation, verification, escalation, and governance. We introduce a formal framework that models AI systems, human evaluators, and hybrid workflows as trajectories in an epistemic state space E defined by eight measurable variables: confidence, trust, uncertainty, verification effort, epistemic risk, cost, diversity, and transparency. State transitions are governed by a small algebra of transformations—judgment, verification, escalation—closed under composition on E, with initialization by a prediction generator and ensembling by an aggregation operator over evaluator collections. We separate admissibility axioms (cost accumulation, well-formedness) from stability conditions (calibration, risk monotonicity, diversity–risk coupling, verification efficacy, marginal cost), and define collapse modes as violations of the latter.Methods: The framework is operationalized through empirical estimators of all eight state variables from system logs, model outputs, and human feedback. We design four experiments testing five trajectory-level claims: MIMIC-IV ICU mortality prediction with clinician override as trust signal (n=3,000), multi-model LLM judge ensembles (simulated and real models via Ollama), recursive verification depth profiling, and pooled stability zone estimation.Results: All five claims are supported. Calibrated model outputs receive 16.7% more clinician trust (H1). In-basin trajectories yield 85.6% trust versus 55.4% out-of-basin (Cohen’s d=0.70, H4). Correlated error grows super-linearly as judge count decreases (b ≈ −1.9, H2). The stability functional peaks at finite verification depth n ∗ =4 (simulated) and n ∗ =2 (real LLMs), confirming diminishing returns to verification (H3). Real-model experiments confirm the self-critique accuracy degradation (88% to 56%) and cross-model recovery (90%).Conclusions: Trust is a trajectory-level property that cannot be reduced to point-wise accuracy. Stability zone membership provides a principled predictor of trust outcomes across clinical and LLM evaluation settings.
